name: Tennessine

discovery.discoverer: Joint Russian-American team, Dubna, Oak Ridge National Laboratory & Vanderbilt University

occurrence: Does not occur naturally; produced only via particle accelerator fusion, atom by atom.
majorUses: No practical applications — pure superheavy-element research
safetyNotes: Intensely radioactive; observed only as individual atoms with sub-second half-lives.
notableCharacteristics: Named after the U.S. state of Tennessee, home to Oak Ridge National Laboratory and Vanderbilt University, key American partners in its discovery — and the second-heaviest halogen ever made, completing Group 17 up to element 117.
ncertRelevance: completes the halogen group's known members
whyHere: Predicted to sit in Group 17 below astatine, tennessine is expected to show even more metallic character than astatine given the trend of increasing metallic behaviour down heavy p-block groups — meaning the 'halogen' at the very bottom of its group may barely resemble chlorine or fluorine at all chemically.
didYouKnow: Making tennessine required an extraordinarily rare berkelium-249 target, which had to be specially manufactured at Oak Ridge National Laboratory and shipped to Russia specifically for the bombardment experiment that created it.
genZNote: A 'halogen' that's predicted to barely act like one at all because it's so heavy and relativistic. The group 17 rebel.
